name: humble-object
intent: Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions.
problem: The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.
context: Applies when an element is hard to test for environmental reasons rather than intrinsic ones: framework callbacks (widgets, dialogs, request handlers, message listeners), entry points (main, server bootstrap) and active objects (threads, processes, timer and interrupt handlers), plus container-managed components whose interfaces the server demands. The logic must be expressible as a computation over data, and the host must keep invoking the element through a stable callback or entry point.
benefits: The decisions become testable by fast synchronous unit tests: no window, event loop, container or thread is needed, so a suite runs in milliseconds and can be written test-first.
Failures localise: a red test names the decision, not a framework stack trace, and a framework upgrade shows up in the few integration tests instead of the whole suite.
The pattern is the standard first move on hard-to-test legacy code: extract, expose or delegate until the logic can be called from a test, then change it safely (Feathers' original motivation).

The remaining adapter is small enough to verify by reading: it reads the context, delegates and applies the result, and can often be inspected faster than it could be tested (Meszaros notes the humble part is frequently left untested on purpose).
All touch points with the host are made visible in one place, which makes porting to another toolkit, container or runtime a bounded change.
Alternative verification collapses into a couple of integration checks around the shell instead of a large slow UI or end-to-end suite.
The collaborator has no framework dependencies, so it can be reused by other hosts (a second UI, a batch job, a CLI) and reviewed as ordinary code.
tradeoffs: It displaces untested code rather than eliminating it: the shell and the translation between framework context and collaborator stay outside the unit tests, so a few integration checks remain mandatory or the blind spot simply moves.
Every callback gains an extra layer and a mapping step (read, translate, delegate, write back); when the decision was three lines, the class, seam and double cost more than the risk they remove.

Humility erodes by default: new behaviour is naturally written where the trigger is, so the shell re-grows unless review keeps treating it as an adapter - the second feature added to a callback is how the pattern dies.

The Poor Man's variant reaches testability by widening visibility (exposing methods or fields), which couples tests to internals and weakens encapsulation; Meszaros lists exactly this as the variant's constraint.

Verifying delegation is delicate in asynchronous hosts: with the callback running on the framework's own thread, assertions inside a mock may never be observed by the test thread (Meszaros warns about the active mock across threads), so the check needs a thread-safe spy or observable state.

Always replacing the collaborator with a double leaves the wiring between shell and real component verified nowhere, and argument-shape assertions make dozens of shell tests break whenever the collaborator is refactored.

participants.responsibility: The framework-facing element (dialog, handler, entry point, worker) the host invokes; it reads the context, translates it into plain data, delegates to the collaborator and applies the result, and holds no decisions of its own.
Plain class, function or module holding the extracted logic; knows nothing about the framework, receives everything as data and returns a result, so tests drive it synchronously.
The interface, trait, function-pointer table or injected function through which the shell calls the collaborator; it is what tests call directly or replace with a double.
The environment that invokes the shell and supplies the context a test cannot create - event loop, request, container, thread - and whose own lifetime rules the shell must respect.
Spy, mock or stub that stands in for the collaborator when the shell's delegation itself is verified (with what data was it called, on which thread, how often).
Drives the collaborator directly with plain data and asserts on its result; the bulk of the suite lives here, with a few integration checks left for the shell.

use_cases: A dialog or screen whose enablement, validation and navigation rules are hard to exercise: extract a presenter or view model, leave the widget showing fields and forwarding events (the Humble Dialog form).
Framework callbacks that mutate business state - HTTP handlers, message listeners, timer or interrupt callbacks - where a thin adapter reads the input and a service decides.
Active objects and executables: a thread or process whose per-request processing is extracted so tests run synchronously instead of sleeping and coordinating (the Humble Executable form).

Transaction boundaries: extract the business logic out of the transaction controller so a test can run the logic and roll the transaction back, leaving only commit/rollback behaviour in the controller (the Humble Transaction Controller form).

Container-managed components: implement the server's interface in a thin adapter and keep the logic in a container-independent class, so the edit-compile-test cycle stays fast (the Humble Container Adapter form).
Legacy code with an overridable or exposed dependency call but no injection point: expose or extract the method first (the Poor Man's form) and only then attempt a test harness.
Entry points: parse arguments, wire dependencies and map the exit code in main, and put the program's decisions in a library function that tests call.

Android Activities/Fragments and Unity MonoBehaviours: extract lifecycle-driven logic into a plain class, leaving the framework component as a thin shell that forwards lifecycle events — enables unit tests without an emulator or device.

React class components and Angular controllers: move state and business logic out of the component into a hook or service, keeping the component as a declarative renderer that delegates all decisions.

Embedded systems interrupt handlers: extract per-interrupt processing into a synchronous function tested with deterministic inputs; the ISR remains a thin vector that disables interrupts and calls the extracted logic.

Database transaction scripts: separate the SQL/transaction orchestration (humble controller) from the business logic (collaborator), so the logic is tested with a connection spy and the wiring is verified by a small number of integration tests.

Event-driven microservices: keep the event-listener adapter minimal (deserialize, delegate) and place all routing and business logic in a synchronous service that tests can drive directly with domain objects.

CLI entry points: extract argument parsing and environment setup from the main method into a plain runner class; the collaborator is tested with fake argv, and the shell only handles OS-level concerns.

Android Jetpack (AndroidX) ViewModel: Google's architecture guidance makes the ViewModel the testable collaborator - it MUST NOT reference Activity, Fragment, View or Context - so screen logic is unit-tested on the JVM with fakes, while the Activity/Fragment stays a humble shell exercised only by instrumentation tests.

WPF / .NET MVVM: Microsoft's guidance prescribes views with empty code-behind - controls bind to ViewModel properties and ICommand implementations (e.g. DelegateCommand) - so enablement, validation and action logic (CanExecute/Execute) are plain classes unit-tested without a window, and XAML binding is covered by a few integration checks.

Unity MonoBehaviour game code: teams extract game rules into plain C# classes unit-tested outside the engine's Play Mode, leaving the MonoBehaviour as a serialized-field shell that forwards Update/FixedUpdate - the Unity community reports this buys fast unit tests at the cost of harder in-engine integration tests, so the shell needs deliberate coverage.
avoid_when: The logic is already reachable by fast tests where it is - extracting a collaborator then only adds indirection.
The element is pure wiring with no decisions (it renames or forwards fields): there is nothing to extract, and a couple of integration tests are cheaper.
The environment already offers a cheap synchronous way to drive the element (a widget test kit, a servlet test container, a headless browser over a stable API); use that instead of restructuring.

The logic is inseparable from live host state (direct manipulation of a canvas or DOM at frame rate): the translation costs more than it saves, so keep the element small and cover it with a few end-to-end tests.
The collaborator would have to call back into the framework for data to do its work: that extraction is in the wrong place - pass the data in or leave the code where it is.
anti_patterns: The almost-humble object: keeping just one branch, default or validation in the shell, so the only logic left in the untestable element is exactly what tests cannot see.
Anemic explosion: one tiny collaborator per callback, each with one caller and one interface, turning a single screen into dozens of classes without a test that ever needed the split.

Visibility widening for tests: making members public or adding test-only flags instead of extracting, so tests pin internals and break on every refactor (the Poor Man's variant done as an access hack).
Mocking the framework: building fake windows, event loops or request objects to keep testing the shell, so the tests exercise the mock and break on framework upgrades.

Delegation-only coverage: the shell is verified against a double and the argument shape is asserted everywhere, while the real collaborator that now owns the behaviour is exercised nowhere near the shell.

Cross-thread assertion theatre: expectations or assertions placed inside a mock invoked on the framework's thread, where failures are never observed and the suite reports green while the shell is broken.

God collaborator: dumping too much logic into a single collaborator, creating a monolithic class that is hard to understand and maintain; the collaborator should have a single responsibility like any other class.
Framework coupling in collaborator: passing framework objects (request, session, widget references) into the collaborator, dragging the environment back into the tests and defeating the extraction.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: handling the environment (I/O, framework lifecycle, asynchrony) is kept apart from deciding what to do.
Single responsibility: the humble object adapts, the collaborator decides - neither does the other's job.

Testability as a first-class design constraint (Feathers, Meszaros): a seam is introduced exactly where the environment blocks verification, and the design is judged by whether it can be driven from a test.
Information hiding: the collaborator learns nothing about the framework; context crosses the seam as plain data.
Encapsulation over exposure: extracting behaviour into a collaborator is preferred to widening visibility so that a test can reach it.
Dependency inversion: the shell depends on an abstract collaborator (interface, trait, function) that a test can replace, not on a concrete component bound to the framework.
best_practices: Extract in two steps - Extract Method to put the decisions in one place, then Extract Class or move to a module - so behaviour is preserved and each step is verifiable (Meszaros describes the refactoring sequence).
Pass the context in as data; if the collaborator needs to ask the host for information, the seam is in the wrong place and the environment leaks back into the tests.
Keep the shell to a fixed sequence (read, translate, delegate, apply) and treat every additional branch as a candidate to move out.

Test the collaborator with plain synchronous tests, and verify delegation on the test thread - through a thread-safe spy, a lazy mock or observable state - never with assertions that run inside the framework's thread.
Keep a small number of integration tests around the shell: the pattern deliberately leaves the adapter untested, so its contract with the framework still needs a check somewhere.
Review for humility: the shell is where behaviour accumulates by default, so each new decision found in a callback or view is treated as a design smell and moved.
Choose the seam deliberately: prefer an explicit collaborator interface (or function) over visibility changes, and keep framework headers out of the collaborator's translation unit.

Treat the seam as a stable interface, not an implementation detail: define the collaborator boundary with an explicit interface (or equivalent language construct) rather than visibility changes, so the contract is naming-visible and refactor-safe (Meszaros, Humelsine).

In MVP/MVVM contexts, keep the Presenter or ViewModel as the collaborator and the View as the humble shell: the presenter holds all state and logic, the view only binds and delegates, enabling synchronous view-model tests without an emulator or device.

For active objects (threads, timers), extract the per-cycle logic into a synchronous collaborator: tests call the logic directly with deterministic input instead of waiting for a thread or relying on sleeps/timeouts, which eliminates race-condition flakiness.

Use Humble Object as a bridge to further refactoring: after extracting a collaborator, apply Move Method to push behaviour into the appropriate domain class rather than accumulating logic in the presenter or service layer.

When multiple UI components share behaviour, extract a shared collaborator rather than duplicating it across presenters: the Humble Object process naturally surfaces duplicated view logic and forces a decision about where it belongs.

Pair with Approval Testing for the shell: because the humble adapter is kept too simple to unit-test, verify its wiring correctness with a single approval test that exercises the real framework integration — this catches wiring regressions without a full end-to-end suite.

The pattern pairs naturally with Dependency Injection: the shell receives the collaborator through an injected interface, making the seam testable with doubles (the interface is the seam, the injection point is the test entry).

Separated Interface enables the seam: define the collaborator's interface away from its implementation so tests can substitute a double without pulling the framework dependency into the test compilation path.

Model-View-Presenter is a direct application of Humble Object: the Presenter is the collaborator (holds all logic), the View is the humble shell (binds and delegates); Passive View is the maximally humble variant.

Presentation Model (predecessor to MVVM) is a Humble Object variant: the view holds no logic, the presentation model holds all state/behaviour, and the view synchronises with it — the view is a humble object.

Model-View-ViewModel applies the Humble Object principle at scale: the ViewModel is the testable collaborator, the View is the humble shell; ViewModel tests run synchronously without a device or emulator.

Functional Core / Imperative Shell is a macro-scale Humble Object: the pure functional core is fully testable and decision-bearing, the imperative shell handles I/O and framework glue and is kept minimal.
Test-Specific Subclass is a Poor Man's Humble Object variant: override framework-dependent methods in a test subclass as a stepping stone before extracting a true collaborator.
Configurable Test Double works with Humble Object at the seam: the double replaces the real collaborator and is configured per-test to simulate framework responses without the real framework.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (2007) - Humble Object (p. 695): extract the logic of a hard-to-test component into a separate easy-to-test component decoupled from its environment; variations Humble Dialog, Humble Executable, Humble Transaction Controller, Humble Container Adapter, Poor Man's and True Humble Object.

Martin Fowler, Humble Object (martinfowler.com, 29 April 2020) - if a program element is hard to test, move as much logic as possible out into testable collaborators - https://martinfowler.com/bliki/HumbleObject.html

Michael Feathers, The Humble Dialog Box (2002, republished with a note by Martin Fowler) - the article that introduced the idea of minimising behaviour in the hard-to-test GUI element - https://martinfowler.com/articles/humble-dialog-box.html

Robert C. Martin, Clean Architecture: A Craftsman's Guide to Software Structure and Design (2017), Chapter 23 'Presenters and Humble Objects' — extends the pattern beyond GUI testing to presenters, view models, and transaction controllers; defines the process as stripping hard-to-test behaviors into a humble module and moving testable behaviors elsewhere.

Jim Humelsine, 'Humble Objects — Designing Code You Don't Hate Testing' (2025) — modern treatment covering Clean Architecture framing, flaky-test mitigation, Clock/Adapter examples, and relation to Façade; includes extensive reference bibliography — https://jhumelsine.github.io/2025/04/14/humble-object.html

Gianmarco David, 'Dumber Views, Smarter ViewModels (aka the Humble Object Pattern)' (2024) — practical MVVM application: keep views (ViewHolders) minimal, push logic into ViewModels; tests for business logic rather than rendering — https://gianmarcodavid.dev/posts/dumber-views/

Garima Singh, 'Testing the Untestable — A step-by-step demonstration of the humble object' (2024) — live refactoring case study applying TDD, dependency injection, and the humble object refactoring sequence to a legacy Android component — https://www.garimasingh.dev/blogs/2024-07-31/testing-the-untestable

Ilija Eftimov, 'TDD Patterns: Humble Object' (2023) — TDD workflow application: test the collaborator first, keep the shell minimal; comparison with other test refactoring patterns — https://ieftimov.com/posts/tdd-humble-object/
DevLead.io, 'Humble Object Pattern' (2020) — practical extraction steps with code examples; anti-patterns of over-applying the pattern — https://devlead.io/DevTips/HumbleObject

Android Developers, 'Recommendations for Android architecture' - official guidance making the ViewModel the lifecycle-agnostic, unit-testable collaborator (no Activity/Fragment/Context references) with the View layer verified by UI tests - https://developer.android.com/topic/architecture/recommendations

Josh Smith, 'WPF Apps With The Model-View-ViewModel Design Pattern' (MSDN Magazine, Feb 2009, on Microsoft Learn) - the canonical statement of MVVM as humble view: empty code-behind, logic behind bound properties and ICommand - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2009/february/patterns-wpf-apps-with-the-model-view-viewmodel-design-pattern

React team, 'Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks' (react.dev) - the officially documented move of extracting stateful logic and external synchronization out of components into a testable plain function - https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks

Unity Discussions, 'Humble Object Pattern: Unit Testing compatibility vs Integration Test compatibility' - practitioner critique: extracting logic from MonoBehaviours complicates in-engine integration tests and can push teams to over-expose internals - https://discussions.unity.com/t/humble-object-pattern-unit-testing-compatibility-vs-integration-test-compatibility/606262
